trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should explain that public multiples matter because they shape private funding expectations and exit math.
It should distinguish between what founders can control and what they cannot.
It should advise founders to focus on fundamentals rather than obsessing over market chatter.
rubric_must_haves: Provides practical founder guidance, not just investor commentary.
Includes at least one example of how multiples affect fundraising, burn, or planning.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that founders cannot ignore public multiples because they influence valuation, fundraising, and investor psychology, but they also should not let them run the company. The right move is to understand the implications, tighten execution, and build the kind of business that works under tougher market assumptions.

trace.answer:
So there’s been a lot of worry among VCs lately around public multiples for SaaS companies.  Not just deceleration overall — though that does make things harder on everyone. But rather, simply the fact that many “growth” stocks have seen their valuations cut by more than half over the past 12-18 months.
In Q4’22, Cloudflare was valued at $37 Billion (!) today, it trades at ~$9B. That’s down -75%!
Datadog was worth $38 billion then, now it’s worth $10B today (-74%)
Monday.com traded at $5.7billion back then. Today it’s worth less than $2billion! (-65%)!! That means Monday’s market cap fell by almost two-thirds!!
Canva was valued at $46 Billion then. Now it’s worth $17 Billion today. So -63%. That’s like a massive haircut. And it wasn’t too long ago they were valued at $86 Billion(!)
And so on
These aren’t start-ups with no revenue yet. These are big, strong public SaaS leaders.  The impact on VC-backed startups isn’t direct per se, but it certainly compounds:
The first concern is how much extra dilution will happen because of this. In general, when founders sell secondary shares (i.e., some of your shares), they don’t get quite full price. Instead, they typically take a discount. How much? It varies, but often these days 30%-50% off what they’d otherwise get if they sold them directly themselves. Why? Because buyers want to buy something cheap, after all. They’re buying those shares from you, the founder(s). This doesn’t really hurt VCs much. It hurts the founders though. Second, VCs do expect folks to work harder during tougher times.
